extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of political philosophy; policymakers and anyone interested in questions of individual liberty and social authority
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th‑century philosophical tract examining the nature and limits of society's legitimate power over the individual, arguing for protection of individuality, free discussion, and limits on social and political authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and limits of legitimate social power
rubrics_metrics.description: “Civil, or Social Liberty: the nature and limits of the power which can be legitimately exercised by society over the individual.” (chapter framing: the central question is where society legitimately may exercise power over individuals.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principal problem is determining where to place the limit between individual independence and social control. The essay treats this as the vital and yet unsettled practical question of the age, requiring fundamental treatment rather than mere feeling or custom-based answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against the tyranny of the majority
rubrics_metrics.description: Society (or the majority) can desire to oppress a part of its number; the will of the people practically means the will of the most numerous or most active part, which may oppress minorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precautions are needed against majority oppression just as against political despotism; democratic accountability does not eliminate the need to protect individuals from majoritarian abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against social (opinion-based) tyranny as distinct from political tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: “Protection ... against the tyranny of the magistrate is not enough: there needs protection also against the tyranny of the prevailing opinion and feeling; against the tendency of society to impose ... its own ideas and practices as rules of conduct on those who dissent from them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social enforcement (ostracism, opinion, moral pressure) can be more penetrating and insidious than legal penalties; the boundary of legitimate collective opinion must be found and defended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of thought and discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Free discussion and freedom of thought must be protected; suppression of opinion hampers the discovery and correction of error and the clearer apprehension of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even false opinions have utility (testing truth, preventing dogmatism); censorship or suppression is an anti-pattern because it deprives society of truth, correction, and fuller understanding. Chapter II explicitly treats this theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between self‑regarding and other‑regarding conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Some actions affect mainly the agent and should not be subject to social or legal coercion; other actions affecting others may justify interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The adjustment between individual independence and social control depends on whether conduct is primarily self-regarding. Coercive measures are appropriate chiefly to prevent harm to others; private conduct not harming others should remain free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuality as an essential element of human well‑being and progress
rubrics_metrics.description: “The grand, leading principle ... is the absolute and essential importance of human development in its richest diversity.” Individual initiative and manifold activities, even antagonistic, are vital for future progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage variety of pursuits and modes of life; enforce against enforced uniformity (political, social, or economic) that would create a dead level and stifle development. Anti-pattern: social systems or customs that dwarf individual initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of law versus opinion in regulating conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Some rules of conduct must be imposed by law, and others by opinion; distinguishing which belongs to which is difficult and central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law should handle the most obvious cases (generally where others are harmed); opinion governs many other matters but must not usurp the role of law or become an illegitimate coercive force. The text warns that custom often masks itself as self-evident truth, complicating the demarcation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that rules and moral judgments be supported by reasons rather than mere preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: People commonly treat their feelings or preferences as sufficient reasons for moral or regulatory judgments; this is inadequate as a justification for compelling others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public rules and social enforcement should rest on articulated reasons, not on the mere fact that 'everybody feels' a certain way. Anti-pattern: appealing only to 'what I like' or class tastes to justify coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward moral rules rooted in class interest or servility
rubrics_metrics.description: Much prevailing morality historically emanates from the interests and feelings of an ascendant class or from servility toward masters or gods, rather than from impartial reasoned concern for society's real interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or proposing rules of conduct, examine whether they reflect particular class interests or prejudices rather than the general good. Be cautious about accepting customary moralities as justifications for coercion.
